reading.quote: And the Lord God commanded the man, "You are free to eat from any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will certainly die."

reading.p: God granted Adam and Eve permission to eat from the trees within the Garden of Eden, providing a rich and abundant plant-based diet. Humanity was originally designed to live on a plant-based diet — in the beginning, God intended for humans to thrive on fruits, vegetables, and herbs, in harmony with nature.

Animals too were given permission to eat plant-based food. Genesis 1:30 states that God provided every green herb as meat for animals, signifying that they also lived on a plant-based diet. Before the time of Noah, both humans and animals were plant-based; prior to the Flood there is no mention of humans eating animals, for both consumed only plant-based foods as God intended.

reading.h2: From Adam to Noah — The Shift in Diet

reading.p: The line from Adam to Noah marks the journey of humanity up to the Great Flood, after which the diet given to humans changed.

list: Adam – the first human created by God.
Seth – the son of Adam and Eve, born after the death of Abel.
Enoch – son of Jared. Enoch "walked with God," and he was taken by God without experiencing death.
Methuselah – son of Enoch. He lived 969 years, the longest recorded lifespan in the Bible.
Noah – son of Lamech. Noah is the righteous man chosen by God to survive the Great Flood and repopulate the Earth after the floodwaters receded.

reading.quote: Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things.

reading.p: Fasting is far more than abstaining from certain foods; it carries deep spiritual purpose. The Church gives us several reasons why we fast.

list: Return to the Original State: It is a way to return to the pure state of humanity before the Fall, mirroring the diet God gave to Adam and Eve.
Spiritual Purification: Fasting cleanses the body and soul, helping believers detach from worldly desires and focus on spiritual growth.
Imitation of Christ and the Prophets: By fasting, Orthodox Christians follow the example set by Jesus Christ and the prophets, who practiced fasting as a means of drawing closer to God.
Self-Control and Discipline: Fasting cultivates self-control and discipline, empowering believers to overcome temptations and strengthen their willpower.
Preparation for Holy Feasts: Fasting prepares the faithful for major feasts by focusing on prayer, reflection, and renewal of faith.

reading.p: Challenges and suffering are part of life, and life has its ups and downs. Yet perspective shapes our experience: when we view challenges as opportunities and let purpose carry us, hardship becomes easier to bear. Perseverance overcomes hardship, and growth comes through struggle. The journey is what matters, not only the end goal.
There are many examples of suffering that bring good things, and they help us understand why fasting is worthwhile.

list: A Mother Giving Birth: The pain and sacrifice of childbirth bring the joy of new life and the deep bond between mother and child.
Physical Training and Muscle Growth: Enduring pain and fatigue during exercise leads to stronger muscles and improved health.
Self-Discipline and Freedom: The discomfort of self-discipline leads to freedom from harmful habits and greater control over one's life.
Fasting and Spiritual Growth: The discomfort of hunger and self-denial during fasting leads to spiritual purification, heightened self-control, and a closer connection to God.

reading.p: We fast every Wednesday and Friday, except during the Fifty Days after the Feast of the Resurrection. Wednesday is kept to remember the betrayal of Judas, and Friday to remember the Crucifixion of Christ.
This fast lasts one day, on the eve of the Feast of Epiphany, to prepare for the celebration of the Epiphany.
This fast lasts three days, two weeks before the Great Lent. It commemorates Jonah's time in the whale's belly and God's salvation.

The Great Lent lasts 55 days before the Feast of the Resurrection. It includes a Preparation Week that precedes the 40 days, the 40 Days of Fasting that reflect Christ's fast in the wilderness, and Pascha Week (Holy Week) leading up to the Resurrection. It engages the faithful in reflection on Christ's suffering, His teachings, and His ultimate Crucifixion and Resurrection.

This fast varies in length, lasting between 10 and 40 days, from the day after Pentecost to July 12, the Feast of the Apostles. It commemorates the Apostles' fasting after receiving the Holy Spirit, as they prepared for their mission to spread the Gospel.
This fast lasts 15 days, from August 7 to August 22, the Feast of the Virgin Mary. It honors the Assumption of the Virgin Mary's body into heaven.
The Nativity Fast lasts 43 or 44 days before the Feast of the Nativity, to spiritually prepare us for the birth of Christ.

studyGuide.overview: This lesson explains the purpose and practice of fasting in the Orthodox Christian faith. It begins with the original plant-based diet God gave in Eden, explains the spiritual reasons we fast and the hidden value of self-denial, and then surveys the seven fasts kept by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
keyPoints: In the beginning God gave humans and animals a plant-based diet; eating meat came only after the Flood (Genesis 9:3).
Fasting is a return to humanity's original, pure state before the Fall.
We fast for spiritual purification, imitation of Christ and the prophets, self-control, and preparation for feasts.
Suffering and self-denial, like childbirth or training, bear good fruit; spiritual growth comes through struggle.
There are seven Orthodox fasts: the Weekly fasts, Gehad (Epiphany), Jonah, Great Lent, the Apostles, the Holy Virgin Mary, and the Nativity.
Wednesday and Friday recall the betrayal of Judas and the Crucifixion of Christ.
reviewQuestions: What kind of diet did God originally give to humans and animals, and what verse marks the change to eating meat?
List the reasons the lesson gives for why Orthodox Christians fast.
How does the 'hidden beauty in suffering' help us understand fasting? Give an example.
Why do we fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, and what is the one exception?
How long is the Great Lent, and what three parts does it include?
What does the Fast of the Holy Virgin Mary commemorate, and when is it kept?

checks: The seven fasts presented match Ethiopian Tewahedo practice
Scriptural basis (Genesis 2:16-17, 1:30, 9:3) used as given in the slides
Assumption of the Virgin Mary honored; Theotokos venerated consistently with the tradition
Purpose of fasting framed as spiritual purification and imitation of Christ — sound
No doctrinal claims about Christ's natures, the Trinity, or the councils were made that would conflict with Tewahedo teaching
